fi-thalassoma-bifasciatum.title: Bluehead Wrasse
fi-thalassoma-bifasciatum.summary: A fast, active Caribbean wrasse that buries itself in sand at night.
rows: About 7 in; wild record 25 cm (9.8 in) TL (FishBase)
Carnivore. Meaty foods; may eat bristleworms or mantis shrimp
Western Atlantic: Bermuda, Florida (USA), southeastern Gulf of Mexico and throughout the Caribbean Sea to northern South America
notes: Wants a sand bed to burrow in at night and plenty of rock (75 gal or more).
Leaves corals and macroalgae alone.

fi-anampses-neoguinaicus.title: China (Black-backed) Wrasse
rows: About 9 in; wild record 20 cm (7.9 in) SL (standard length) (FishBase)
Juveniles can be kept together but may fight as adults
Carnivore. Small meaty foods; may pick at fanworms and ornamental crustaceans
Western Pacific: Philippines and Taiwan to Fiji, north to the Izu Islands, south to the Great Barrier Reef and New Caledonia
notes: Needs 120 gal or more with live rock to forage.

fi-labroides-dimidiatus.title: Cleaner Wrasse
fi-labroides-dimidiatus.summary: The Bluestreak Cleaner Wrasse sets up a cleaning station and picks parasites off other fish, even inside their mouths and gills.
rows: About 5½ in; wild record 14 cm (5.5 in) TL (FishBase)
Carnivore. Small amounts of enriched mysis and brine shrimp several times a day; later flake and tiny pellets
Indo-Pacific: Persian Gulf; Red Sea and East Africa to the Line, Marquesas, and Ducie islands, north to southern Japan, south to Lord Howe and Rapa islands
notes: Very active; keep with fish of different shape and color.
warn: Advanced care: recommended only for experienced keepers.
Jumps; use a tight lid and cover overflow boxes.

fi-choerodon-fasciatus.title: Harlequin Tuskfish
fi-choerodon-fasciatus.summary: A colorful wrasse with bright blue tusk-like teeth used to crunch invertebrates.
rows: About 10 in; wild record 30 cm (11.8 in) TL (FishBase)
With caution. Leaves corals alone but eats small crustaceans
Western Pacific: disjunct distribution, Ryukyus to Taiwan, then from New Caledonia to Queensland, Australia
notes: Needs 125 gal or more with moderately aggressive tankmates.

fi-thalassoma-lunare.title: Lunare Wrasse
fi-thalassoma-lunare.summary: A large, active wrasse, also called the Lyretail Wrasse.
rows: About 10 in; wild record 45 cm (17.7 in) TL (FishBase)
Carnivore. Frozen mysis, enriched brine shrimp, flake and pellets
Indo-Pacific: Red Sea and East Africa to the Line Islands, north to southern Japan, south to Lord Howe Island and northern New Zealand
notes: Eats mantis shrimp and bristleworms but not corals.
Best with larger, assertive tankmates in 125 gal or more.

fi-thalassoma-lutescens.title: Banana Wrasse (Sunset Wrasse)
fi-thalassoma-lutescens.summary: A large, restless Indo-Pacific wrasse. Females and young are yellow, and males turn blue-green with a pink-and-green striped head.
rows: About 12 in (Top Shelf adult size); wild record 30 cm (11.8 in) TL (FishBase)
Carnivore. Foods: mysis shrimp, brine shrimp, krill, chopped prawn, clam and mussel, squid, marine pellets, marine flakes
Indo-Pacific: Sri Lanka to Ducie Island, north to southern Japan and the Hawaiian Islands, south to southeastern Australia, Lord Howe Island, the Kermadec Islands
notes: Pair with active, tough fish (tangs, puffers, larger angels); gobies, firefish and flasher wrasses are poor company. Not safe with shrimp, crabs and other small invertebrates.

fi-novaculichthys-taeniourus.title: Dragon Wrasse (Rockmover Wrasse)
fi-novaculichthys-taeniourus.summary: A big wrasse whose juveniles look like a drifting scrap of algae, with long front dorsal spines. Adults are greenish-brown and flip over rocks and rubble to hunt.
rows: About 12 in (Top Shelf adult size); wild record 30 cm (11.8 in) TL (FishBase)
Carnivore. Foods: mysis shrimp, krill, enriched brine shrimp, chopped shrimp or prawn, squid, clam and mussel, fish flesh, marine pellets
Indo-Pacific: Red Sea to South Africa and the Tuamoto Islands, north to Ryukyu and Hawaiian islands, south to Lord Howe Island
notes: It flips and shoves rocks while foraging and buries itself in sand at night or when startled: secure the rockwork and give a sand bed.
Not reef safe: eats shrimp, crabs, snails, starfish, urchins and worms, and small or timid fish.

fi-coris-formosa.title: Formosa Coris Wrasse (Queen Coris)
fi-coris-formosa.summary: A large Indian Ocean wrasse that changes a lot with age: juveniles are orange with white bars outlined in black, while adults turn dark with black spots and a blue line across an orange face.
rows: About 20–24 in (Saltwaterfish.com adult size); wild record 60 cm (23.6 in) TL (FishBase)
Carnivore: hunts crabs, shrimp, urchins and small invertebrates; feed enriched frozen mysis and brine shrimp, other meaty foods, flake and pellets
Western Indian Ocean: southern Red Sea to Natal, South Africa and east to Sri Lanka
notes: Needs a deep sand bed (about 4–6 in) to bury itself at night, and a tight lid.
It turns over rocks looking for food.
warn: Not reef safe; it eats invertebrates.

fi-halichoeres-melanurus.title: Hoeven's Wrasse (Tail-spot Wrasse)
fi-halichoeres-melanurus.summary: A small Indo-Pacific wrasse that buries itself in the sand to sleep or hide. It eats flatworms, but also snails and small crustaceans.
rows: Mostly peaceful; may squabble with similar wrasses
A pair, or one male with several females
With caution: fine with corals but eats snails, tubeworms and small shrimp
Small meaty foods: mysis, brine shrimp, copepods and other small invertebrates
Indo-Pacific: Bali and Western Australia to Samoa, north to Japan
notes: Keep the tank covered: it is known to jump.
Needs at least 2 in (5 cm) of sand to bury in.
Known to eat flatworms.

fi-cheilinus-oxycephalus.title: Snooty Wrasse (Maori Snooty Wrasse)
fi-cheilinus-oxycephalus.summary: A secretive Indo-Pacific wrasse that rarely strays far from cover. It eats snails and crustaceans, so it suits fish-only tanks rather than reefs with cleanup crews.
rows: Best kept as the only one of its kind
Varied meaty foods (shrimp, mysis, krill); live food can help it start eating
Indo-Pacific: East Africa to the Marquesas and Society Islands
notes: Hides a lot at first; give it plenty of rockwork and leave it undisturbed.
Secure rockwork: it rearranges rocks and sand.

fi-gomphosus-varius.title: Bird Wrasse
fi-gomphosus-varius.summary: A fast-swimming Indo-Pacific wrasse; males are green and females paler and duller. Very active and hardy, it needs a large tank with open swimming room.
rows: Active; may be aggressive toward similar fish
Singly, or as a pair added together
With caution: eats shrimp, crabs, snails, small clams and may nip larger clams
Varied meaty foods: shrimp, mysis, krill and other crustaceans
Indo-Pacific: Cocos-Keeling to Hawaii, north to southern Japan
notes: Keep the tank covered: it is known to jump.
Females can change into males.

fi-thalassoma-jansenii.title: Jansen's Wrasse
fi-thalassoma-jansenii.summary: A bold black, white and yellow banded wrasse from the Indo-West Pacific. Hardy but aggressive, it grows large and eats small invertebrates and fish.
rows: Best kept as the only one of its kind
With caution: eats shrimp, worms, snails and may nip clams
Varied meaty foods: shrimp, mysis, krill and zooplankton
Indo-West Pacific: Maldives to Fiji, north to southern Japan
notes: Keep the tank covered: it is known to jump.

fi-halichoeres-leucoxanthus.title: Lemon Meringue Wrasse (Canarytop / White Belly Wrasse)
fi-halichoeres-leucoxanthus.summary: A small Indian Ocean wrasse that is bright yellow on top and white below, with black eyespots on the fins. It buries itself in the sand to sleep each night.
rows: Mostly peaceful; can quarrel with other wrasses
With caution: may pick at small snails, hermit crabs and clams
Carnivore: meaty frozen foods; picks pods off rock and sand
Indian Ocean (including Indonesia, Sri Lanka and Christmas Island)
notes: Needs a sand bed at least a few inches deep to dive into at night.
Keep the tank covered: it is known to jump.
May be slow to accept flakes or pellets; start with frozen foods.
